analysis.title: Global Technology: Global Data Center Capacity update: Increasing capacity estimates
key_insights: GS raises its global data center capacity forecast to 273GW by 2030 from 217GW in its July 2026 update, using 451 Research's tracker data through 2Q26. That implies growth from about 103GW in 2025 at a 21% 2025-2030 CAGR, or 170GW of net additions after 2025.
Net additions are forecast at 25GW in 2026, 32GW in 2027 and 35GW in 2028. GS does not expect the pace of net additions to moderate in the medium term.

Most of the increase comes from scaling up 451 Research's outer-year forecasts to account for projects not yet announced. 2Q26 451 forecasts for global net adds were also revised up 8% in 2026 and 14% in 2027 and 2028 versus the 1Q26 update.
170GW of net additions implies about $8.5tn of cumulative capex over 5 years at an assumed $50B/GW all-in. GS notes IT infrastructure costs continue to see upward pressure.

The $8.5tn is above the roughly $1.51tn per year of forecast average US hyperscaler capex (Visible Alpha consensus). GS says that consensus has historically been revised higher and excludes international hyperscalers such as Alibaba and Tencent, private AI lab capex and data center platform capex.
For the US, GS forecasts 152GW of capacity by 2030 (125GW prior), or 103GW of additions after 2025. 2Q26 451 US net-add forecasts were revised up 2% in 2026, 5% in 2027 and 12% in 2028 versus 1Q26.
GS raised its US net-add estimates by 56% in 2029 and 180% in 2030 versus its last update, from scaling up unannounced projects.

US cloud/neocloud/crypto/wholesale/retail net adds were revised up by 11.8GW cumulatively over 2026-2030, which GS reads as the rapid scaling of neocloud providers to support GPU demand. US hyperscaler net adds were revised up by 9.4GW cumulatively over the same period.

HPC data centers (typically tied to AI workloads), meaning projects of 75MW or more, are expected to be about 66% of global net adds by 2028 and 75% of US net adds by 2028. The US is expected to account for about 60-70% of global net adds through 2030.
Exhibit 5 shows greater visibility into APAC net adds, while Europe sees increased net adds in the outer years.

Power supply is a constraint. Microsoft exited a lease commitment because of a delayed ready-for-service date tied to power supply (WSJ, 10/19/2026), and Oracle's New Mexico project has faced power permitting challenges (WSJ, 9/25/2026). Visibility into secured power is becoming more important.

Community and regulatory risk is rising. Governors in Texas and Pennsylvania effectively paused their fast-track approval processes for data centers. GS sees the main burden falling on speculative builds, with ongoing headline risk and potentially slower development.

HPC data center construction is typically 80-90% loan-to-cost, so returns are highly sensitive to compression in the debt yield spread. GS expects more focus on lease duration and tenant credit quality, with asset-backed debt on high-quality projects offering 15-30 year contracted cash flows from investment-grade tenants.

GS says investors have pushed back that its capacity estimates are conservative, which it attributes to the higher barrier for a project to enter 451 Research's pipeline. It expects the added execution risk to hit projects not originally in its forecasts hardest.

sector_views.rationale: GS sees potential for sustained, outsized capacity growth through projects with high visibility into power and permitting, while acknowledging rising execution risk.

earnings_insights: Consensus hyperscaler and AI-player capex (Visible Alpha, estimates as of 10/30/2026) totals $918,177mn in 2026E, $1,518,163mn in 2027E, $1,666,889mn in 2028E, $1,708,969mn in 2029E and $1,742,766mn in 2030E. These are consensus estimates, not reported results. Y/y growth is 101% in 2026E, 65% in 2027E, 10% in 2028E, 3% in 2029E and 2% in 2030E.

Consensus 2026E capex by company, in $mn: AMZN 228,406; META 138,411; GOOGL 201,011; MSFT 155,010; ORCL 74,557; SPCX 74,452; CRWV 35,666; AAPL 10,664. Consensus 2027E: AMZN 300,605; META 214,307; GOOGL 331,600; MSFT 213,051; ORCL 100,146; SPCX 298,100; CRWV 47,387; AAPL 12,967.
Consensus for ORCL capex peaks in 2027E at $100,146mn and falls to $73,370mn by 2030E, while the other listed names are still rising or flat in 2030E.
crypto_views: Crypto miners are grouped with cloud, neocloud, wholesale and retail providers in GS's US net-add category, which saw the largest upward revisions (+11.8GW cumulative over 2026-2030).
risk_factors: Power supply constraints and delayed ready-for-service dates, including Microsoft's lease exit and Oracle's New Mexico permitting issues.
Regulatory uncertainty, including the Texas and Pennsylvania pauses on fast-track data center approvals.
Community pushback (NIMBY concerns, perceived societal and economic impact of AI, transparency of the development process) that GS Sustain says may not be fully allayed by proposed solutions.
High leverage of 80-90% loan-to-cost on HPC builds, with returns sensitive to the debt yield spread and to pressure on hyperscaler bond yields.
Execution risk is expected to fall disproportionately on projects not originally in the forecasts, mainly speculative builds.
Cost inflation: IT infrastructure costs continue to see upward pressure, which raises the capex per GW.
charts_described: Exhibit 1: Global data center capacity scales to about 273GW by 2030, +170GW versus 2025.
Exhibit 2: Global capacity forecasts for 2026-2030 have been raised by 11% on average versus 1Q26, 17% versus 4Q25 and 26% versus 3Q25.
Exhibit 6: US data center capacity grows to about 152GW by 2030, +103GW from 2025.
Exhibit 7: US net add forecasts have been revised up by 51% on average versus 1Q26, 69% versus 4Q25 and 102% versus 3Q25.
Exhibit 10: Consensus AI/Cloud player capex reaches about $1.74 trillion by 2030, a 31% 2025-2030 CAGR.

tension_points.bull_case: GS raises its 2030 global capacity forecast to 273GW, sees net adds of 25-35GW a year not moderating, and says investors view its estimates as conservative given the high bar for inclusion in 451 Research's pipeline.
tension_points.bear_case: Power supply delays (Microsoft's lease exit, Oracle's New Mexico permitting), Texas and Pennsylvania pauses on fast-track approvals, community pushback and 80-90% loan-to-cost leverage raise execution risk, especially for speculative builds.

theme_stances.key_argument: Capacity net adds should stay elevated through projects with high visibility into power and permitting, despite rising execution risk.
theme_stances.evidence: we still see potential for sustained, outsized growth in capacity

theme_stances.key_argument: Power supply, regulatory uncertainty and high leverage will hit speculative projects hardest.
theme_stances.evidence: rising execution risk of building and delivering data centers
